Chapter 4: Questioning Authority and the Power of Speaking Up
There comes a moment when the rules just don’t add up anymore—when staying quiet actually feels riskier than finally speaking your mind.
If you grew up being told to trust authority, to follow the crowd, realizing this can be both freeing and honestly, a little terrifying.
You see, the church’s grip was never just about what you believed—it was about getting people to obey. Members learned early on: don’t question the leaders, and believe that the organization’s needs always come first.
If you had doubts, you were seen as weak. If you asked questions, you were seen as a threat. That pressure to fit in was everywhere—sometimes it was subtle, other times, it came with a not-so-subtle threat.
But after a while, those little cracks in the perfect picture start to show. You’d hear stories—about people getting mistreated, about leaders abusing their power, about folks who got shunned for simply asking the wrong thing.
And let’s be honest, the official stories almost never lined up with what was really happening. The more you saw, the harder it became to pretend everything was okay.
Deciding to speak up? It doesn’t usually happen in one big, dramatic moment. It starts quietly—maybe you ask a question you’re not supposed to, or you break a rule that doesn’t feel right, or you share a private conversation with someone you trust.
Every little act brings its own mix of relief and fear. Relief, because you’re finally being true to yourself—refusing to go along with what you know is wrong. And fear—because you know exactly what’s at stake: losing your status, your community, even your family.
Now, if you’re someone in the public eye, the risks get even bigger. The church’s influence stretches way beyond its own walls. Speaking up can put your career, your friendships, and your reputation on the line—not just your personal relationships, but everything you’ve worked hard to build.
But here’s the thing—the need to be honest eventually gets too loud to ignore. The cover-ups, the pressure to fit in, the constant lying—it wears you down. At some point, you realize that staying silent just means you’re letting it all continue, and real change only happens when someone has the guts to speak up.
Most people never have to stare down the full force of an institution like that. But if you do, it changes you. It’s scary. It’s painful. But it’s also the moment you start to feel free—when you take back your life by telling the truth, even if it costs you.
And looking back, something becomes really clear. The real problem isn’t people who ask questions—it’s the ones who demand silence.
So if there’s one thing to remember, it’s this: the courage to speak up, to challenge authority, that’s what actually moves the world forward.
